Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75–85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.
entries.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted at IEEE IECON 2026

entries.title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
entries.abstract: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to 4× more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.
entries.comment: Preprint. 22 pages, 21 figures

entries.title: The Limit Is in the Input, Not the Model: State-Dependent Command Safety in Natural-Language Interfaces to Industrial Controllers
entries.abstract: Language models judging commands to industrial controllers may not receive machine state, the equipment's current condition. The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed commands and another always denied them. Their overall (raw) accuracies differed by 32 percentage points; both scored 50% balanced accuracy, which weights safe and unsafe cases equally, and no correct pairs. A rule evaluator matched all 15 pairs by applying the same rules that supplied the expected answers; this is not an independent safety test. The audit complements systems that check actions against safety rules: it checks whether the model receives the information needed for those decisions. This helps evaluators separate missing-input problems from model errors. These small-sample scores do not establish general model reliability.
entries.comment: 8 pages. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW), 6th Machine Learning for Cybersecurity (MLC) Workshop

entries.title: Gradient-Based Defensive Poisoning Against System Identification Attacks on Cyber-Physical Systems
entries.abstract: AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. Because covertness depends on the accuracy of the identified model, degrading that accuracy is a viable countermeasure. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.
entries.comment: Presented at the 2026 IEEE International Workshop on Technologies for Defense and Security (TechDefense 2026), Torino, Italy, November 4-6, 2026

entries.title: ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
entries.abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.
entries.comment: ChainIT white paper CIT-TT-EWP-2.1. 29 pages, 4 figures. Companion papers: Provable Authority (arXiv:2610.22899), Provable Compliance (arXiv:2610.22913). Project page: https://chainit.com/white-papers/

entries.title: Robust, Lightweight Locally Differentially Private Histogram Estimation and the Role of Dropout Attacks
entries.abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.

entries.title: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty
entries.abstract: State machine replication protocols are usually proven secure in the honest-Byzantine setting, which requires an honest supermajority of validators. Deployed systems offer no such guarantee: validators participate for profit and may deviate from the protocol whenever doing so increases their gains. In our work, every validator is rational or Byzantine, and none is honest. Rational validators may collude with each other and with the Byzantine ones, who may also bribe them to deviate. Known impossibility results show that, without honest validators, clients that decide whether to accept a transaction based on a non-interactive certificate and without further communication cannot be kept safe. To bypass these results, we let clients relay the certificates they receive to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. We also assume that one full node, whose identity is unknown, is honest and always online. Under this assumption, we build a finalization layer over any certifiable quorum-based protocol in a synchronous network. Clients run an existing freezing gadget and fetch past certificates from the honest full node, which makes the protocol always-safe: no two honest clients confirm conflicting ledgers, for any strategy of the validators. We incentivize participation through rewards, which the adversary may use to bribe rational validators into censoring transactions. In this setting, we formalize censorship and characterize it tightly: paying only with his rewards, the adversary censors less than a fraction of the available fees at each height, where is the fraction of the quorum he signs, and every coin of censorship beyond that comes from his own funds.

entries.title: SCR: Detecting Backdoor-Poisoned Samples through Clean-Reference Residuals
entries.abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which adversaries manipulate model predictions by injecting poisoned samples into training data. Detecting these samples remains challenging because legitimate semantic variation can obscure poisoning-related signals in learned representations. Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. In this paper, we propose Semantic Counterfactual Residualization (SCR), which uses a small set of clean reference samples to account for benign variation through sample-specific feature reconstruction. SCR identifies poisoned samples by detecting coherent deviations from these clean baselines, without requiring prior knowledge of the attacks. We evaluate SCR through experiments covering twelve dirty-label and clean-label attacks across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. With a small clean-reference set, SCR achieves attack-averaged true positive rates above 99.5% and false positive rates below 2% on each dataset, outperforming eight representative detection baselines in macro-TPR.

entries.title: RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback
entries.abstract: Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures

entries.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
entries.abstract: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate — reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs. 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed — DeepSeek V4 Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6 Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.
entries.comment: Presented at NeurIPS Workshops: (1) Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond, and (2) The 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026

entries.title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
entries.abstract: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8% to 48.4%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.
entries.comment: 21 pages, 9 figures

entries.title: Drift-Aware Explainable Prioritization for Windows PE Malware Forensic Triage with Semantic Consistency Checks
entries.abstract: Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) malware detectors usually return a bare score that neither explains why a file deserves attention nor signals when changing data make the model unreliable. We present a framework for Windows Portable Executable (PE) malware forensic triage that works only on pre-extracted static features and never executes malware. A calibrated maliciousness score sets each file's triage priority, and a per-sample feature attribution explains the prediction. A per-sample consistency score measures whether the top attributed features agree with documented behaviors from the Malware Behavior Catalog (MBC) and MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge (ATT&CK), where the available features support such interpretation. Conformal evaluation and statistical distribution tests flag drift. Each file receives one investigator-oriented triage output. The evaluation protocol, specified before testing, uses a time-ordered split of EMBER2024 as the primary dataset and BODMAS for family disjoint checks, and compares every component with simple baselines on predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and robustness over time.

entries.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
entries.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 6 figures

entries.title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
entries.abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Project page at https://stevendamianakis.github.io/autopi-site/ and code at https://github.com/stevendamianakis/autopi

entries.title: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery from Obfuscated KV Caches
entries.abstract: LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming secret reuse scope as the operative vulnerability. We further confirm orbit collapse on two other open-source defenses: the sequence-permutation implementation of Thomas et al. and PermLLM. The KV-Cloak developers invited a detailed report through their private vulnerability reporting channel.
entries.comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables

entries.title: Retained Encrypted Search with Certified Split Joins
entries.abstract: Retaining encrypted search across data edits and worker replacement requires separating computational validity from current release authority. We give exact Hamming search with at most one authorized decryption and decoding attempt per query preparation. Under authenticated prescribed execution, exclusive nonrollback owner state, an ideal public seed-expansion interface and a stated observation model, we reduce bounded adaptive privacy to ordinary ring learning with errors (Ring-LWE). Expanded second components depend only on public masks and fixed maps, independently of queries and the fresh database key. This compiler invariant permits a retained split join against a smaller-modulus encrypted database. A simultaneous bound on the completed circuit covers a finite honest reservation family, including adaptive queries and slot selection, with explicit statistical correctness and privacy losses. In three post-calibration local CPU comparisons on 32,768 vectors of 512 bits, the 60-bit-join construction takes a median 9.825 s for an end-to-end two-query workload, versus 12.159 s for the optimized full-source-modulus baseline. These times include setup, transfers, preparation and private completion. They are local implementation results, not deployment or concrete-security claims.

entries.title: PMKPIR: Parallel Multi-Keyword PIR with Interleaved Batching for Private Boolean Retrieval
entries.abstract: Keyword Private Information Retrieval (Keyword PIR) allows users to retrieve data associated with specific keywords from a database while protecting query privacy. However, existing Keyword PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval either incur high computational overhead due to multiple database traversals, or fail to support universal boolean computation. We propose PMKPIR, a novel keyword PIR scheme supporting both parallel multi-keyword queries and universal boolean computation. We utilize the single instruction multiple data (SIMD) capability of BFV homomorphic encryption to propose an interleaved batching method, and design IBPIR based on this method, achieving the private matching of multiple keywords in a single database traversal. Furthermore, we design a boolean query processing method, extending the parallel capability of interleaved batching from keyword querying to boolean query computation, to support universal boolean computation and accelerate boolean operations. Building upon IBPIR, we integrate this method to further design PMKPIR. To the best of our knowledge, PMKPIR is the first Keyword PIR scheme to support multi-keyword batch matching within boolean queries. Security analysis demonstrates that, consistent with existing PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval, PMKPIR preserves the core security guarantees of classic PIR. Compared with state-of-the-art schemes, PMKPIR reduces query time, communication overhead, storage overhead, and peak memory by up to 79.06%, 75.00%, 97.92%, and 80.26%, respectively.

entries.title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
entries.abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31% to 101.61%, but Qwen falls to 61.99% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.

entries.title: Erased but Recoverable: On the Fragility of Concept Erasure Under Fine-Tuning
entries.abstract: Existing concept erasure methods for text-to-image diffusion models primarily focus on suppressing target concepts while preserving non-target generation quality. However, in practical applications, open-source diffusion models are often further adapted through DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion. Such adaptations can reshape internal representations, thereby weakening or even reversing the erasure effects achieved by existing methods. We identify erasure persistence as a key yet underexplored dimension of concept erasure and analyze how downstream fine-tuning reshapes internal representations. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning of the original model does not uniformly modify the model, but preserves certain high-contribution structures, particularly attention heads with stable output subspaces and response magnitudes. We also observe that, after downstream fine-tuning of concept-erased models, these heads' output representations more readily realign with their pretrained counterparts. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stable-Head-Aware Concept Erasure (SHACE), which improves erasure persistence by preserving stable attention structures during concept erasure. SHACE identifies stability-critical attention heads through Attention-Head Stability Profiling and keeps their corresponding parameter blocks unchanged during erasure via Stable-Head Gradient Preservation. Extensive experiments show that SHACE improves resistance to concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression and non-target generation quality.

entries.title: Guarding the Kingdom of Skill-Based Agents in the AI Dynasty of Computation: Control-Flow Integrity for Agent Skills
entries.abstract: Control-flow integrity (CFI) confines a program to a control-flow graph fixed ahead of time. Procedural agent skills move this control flow into prompt text, and a large language model (LLM) agent decides at runtime whether each step runs in its reasoning, a tool call, or a script. The procedure's control skeleton survives, but its enforceability depends on where each step runs. Many violations, such as overwriting a file before validation, use only operations the skill requires, so permission allowlists admit them. A deviating or prompt-injected model can also evade a monitor by regime migration, for example by claiming that a check passed. We present SkillCFI, which carries CFI over to skill-based agents. Its compiler confines LLM interpretation to compile time and derives the agent's instructions and an executable contract from one skill. By a formal enforceability criterion, it enforces obligations whose evidence crosses the tool boundary and rejects a skill whose mandatory obligation leaves nothing to check. A deterministic runtime enforcer admits a tool request only on trusted evidence and refuses unmediated channels such as inline scripts, so admitted traces follow the contract whatever the model proposes. On eight self-written skills, no compiled contract permits more than its source under 24 source mutations. In 770 agent sessions, SkillCFI blocks before dispatch all 240 such violations, which an allowlist admits, and normal tasks complete nearly as often as without it. Listing the next legal steps in a refusal raises recovery from 21% to 65%. Checking takes about 2% of task time, and a compact command form cuts session slowdown from 1.32 times to 1.08 times. None of 53 public skills is accepted as written. The compiler's diagnostics point to interfaces rather than workflows and guided seven into enforceable contracts.

entries.title: PULSAR-V: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation for RISC-V
entries.abstract: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. We present PULSAR-V, a post-update attestation architecture which binds the authenticated update commit to the effective permissions and immutability of both gates (PMP/EPMP on the CPU, the I/O policy mediating DMA), sampled at the commit and at attestation, the I/O gate latching its own commit-time state in hardware. In a RISC-V SoC prototyped on a ZCU102 FPGA (CV32E40S core with 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard), a 256-byte write from the board's Arm DMA engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image: every conventional claim stays true, and PULSAR-V rejects the device on its I/O-policy evidence alone. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. The gate and its commit latch cost 436 LUTs, 4.6% of the SoC, and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles independent of image size, 41x less than re-hashing 16 KiB.

entries.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices
entries.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
entries.comment: Withdrawn by the submitter because not all co-authors agreed to the posting of this preprint

entries.title: PIVOT: Distribution-Preserving Multi-BitWatermarking with Minimax-Optimal Scoring
entries.abstract: As LLM-generated content becomes increasingly widespread, reliable attribution calls for multi-bit watermarks that embed recoverable messages without distorting the output distribution. We introduce PIVOT, a multi-bit watermark with model-free verification based on mirrored rank-interval sampling. At each generation step, PIVOT uses a keyed pseudorandom scalar and a secret permutation of the vocabulary. The message bit determines whether next-token probability intervals are arranged in forward or reverse secret-rank order. Sampling from these mirrored layouts preserves every token probability exactly while inducing an opposite-signed dependence between the scalar and the sampled token's secret rank. This dependence yields a pivotal rank statistic whose null distribution is invariant to the unknown next-token law, enabling model-free calibration and decoding. We formulate joint watermark detection and message recovery as a multiple-hypothesis testing problem, derive a moment-robust minimax-optimal detection score over a relaxed moment class, and establish finite-sample recovery guarantees. Extensive experiments on two representative large language models validate the effectiveness of PIVOT, demonstrating reliable watermark detection and message recovery while preserving the generator's output distribution.

entries.title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
entries.abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.

entries.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
entries.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zwang-devv/intent-contracts

entries.title: When Do Decision Models Help LLM-Driven Network Discovery?
entries.abstract: Network discovery, the identification of live hosts and their exposed services, is the first phase of every penetration test, and it is increasingly automated by harnesses driven by large language models (LLMs). To mitigate hallucinated or unsafe commands, recent work proposes inserting fast, non-generative decision models to validate actions prior to execution. This paper quantifies whether such validation improves discovery across three network scales (n = 10, 100, and 1,000) in a simulation calibrated on a 30-node containerized testbed. Our findings show that chunked batch dispatch recovers 92% to 100% of open ports in large-scale networks, whereas single-host dispatch collapses to under 6% due to context saturation and scan latency. Furthermore, at the measured proposal quality of the local model, decision gating increases its port recall from 75.5% to 89.0% on small networks and intercepts costly decoy tarpits, but it imposes additional latency on frontier models during early host discovery.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 3rd International Symposium on Parallel Computing and Distributed Systems (PCDS 2026) on November 16-18, 2026 in Singapore

entries.title: Smoothing and Learning for Movement-Robust RSS-Based Spoofing Detection
entries.abstract: Physical-layer spoofing detection identifies an attacker who impersonates a legitimate wireless user by checking whether transmissions claiming the same identity originate from different locations, using the received signal strength (RSS) measured at several receivers. A recent scheme by Romero et al. makes this approach robust to user movement by combining a neural-network position-change detector (PCD) with community detection on a graph of frames and a fixed threshold on a hand-crafted test statistic. I study two modifications to this scheme. First, I smooth the sequence of PCD scores with a median or Gaussian temporal filter before thresholding. Second, I replace the fixed decision threshold with a supervised classifier operating on six statistical features of the region sequence produced by community detection. On real indoor RSS measurements from 52 transmitter locations, Gaussian filtering raises PCD accuracy from 0.870 to 0.921 when the PCD is trained on 10 locations and from 0.905 to 0.925 when trained on 40. On synthetic attack and no-attack sequences built from the same measurements, evaluated on a held-out test set of 1,679 sequences, the best classifier (XGBoost) reaches an accuracy of 0.949 and an F1 score of 0.940, and random forests reach an AUC of 0.99. The detector separates static attackers almost perfectly but misses about a third of attacks in which two transmitters move simultaneously, which produce region sequences similar to those of a single moving user.

entries.title: Weighing the Envelope: Component Weight and Arbitration in Envelope-Layer Defenses for a Single LLM Agent
entries.abstract: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

entries.title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
entries.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.

entries.title: Slice Isolation-as-a-Service: An Isolation Mechanism to Proactively Defend Cross-Slice Attacks in 5G-Advanced and Beyond
entries.abstract: As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. Empirical evaluations under active volumetric flooding and the recently discovered GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks reveal that shared and Virtualized Network Function (VNF)-only isolation fail catastrophically, suffering up to 30% packet loss and complete bandwidth starvation. Our results prove that MINLP-driven strict physical isolation successfully neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability for mission-critical slices, confirming our isolation framework as a crucial proactive defense for next-generation core networks.

entries.title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
entries.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: complete attention hijacking, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and partial attention hijacking, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose DetectViT, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64–128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of 100% and a false positive rate of 0.17% on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.
entries.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026

entries.title: Authenticating IoT Data on Ethereum after Pectra and Fusaka: A Cost Study of Signature Schemes, Batching and Anchoring for Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
entries.abstract: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at 2²⁴. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.
entries.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24328819

entries.title: Expressiveness and Convertibility of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
entries.abstract: Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.

entries.title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites
entries.abstract: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.

entries.title: Data Poisoning Attacks to Locally Differentially Private Triangle Counting Protocols
entries.abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a crucial paradigm for privacy-preserving graph analytics, enabling graph analytics tasks such as subgraph counting without requiring a trusted curator. However, while LDP provides strong privacy guarantees, the integrity and robustness of LDP subgraph counting protocols in the presence of malicious participants remain poorly understood. In particular, since data are randomized locally before collection, it is inherently difficult to distinguish malicious users from honest ones based solely on their submitted reports, and small, protocol-compliant local manipulations can be systematically amplified through reconstruction and calibration into large global estimation bias. In this paper, we use LDP triangle counting as a representative task to characterize the vulnerability of LDP subgraph counting to data poisoning attacks. For both non-interactive and interactive LDP triangle counting protocols, we analyze their attack surfaces and develop a unified gain-driven framework that captures how adversarial users can manipulate calibrated subgraph count estimates, which we instantiate on representative protocols of both types. Extensive experiments on four real-world graph datasets demonstrate that these attacks can significantly distort triangle count estimates across different protocols and adversarial settings. Moreover, we show that existing and straightforward defenses are insufficient to mitigate these attacks, underscoring the need for robustness mechanisms tailored to LDP subgraph counting.
entries.comment: Accepted by ICDE 2027

entries.title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
entries.abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field F_p, and the rational (2,2)-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let C be such a curve, with Jacobian J and Frobenius endomorphism π. We show that π² = p α_* for a unique automorphism α of C over F_p whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For p ≥7 this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on p, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of F_p-rational (2,2)-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on J[2] is determined by p 8. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of ζ_Q(√p)(-1), for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For π² = ±p the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order p^(-1/2)(1+L(1,χ)), where χ is the quadratic character of Q(√(-p)). All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes 7 ≤p ≤173. Finally we describe the graph of F_p-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.
entries.comment: 55 pages, 9 tables. Code, logs and data: [Zenodo DOI, add after upload]

entries.title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
entries.abstract: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

entries.title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
entries.abstract: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures

entries.title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
entries.abstract: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

entries.title: Protecting Web Applications using a Multimodal AI-based System for Classifying Web Injection Attacks
entries.abstract: Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.
entries.comment: 19 pages, 5 figures

entries.title: A-Tag: Cryptographic File Tagging with Enforced Live Human Presence
entries.abstract: The increasing autonomy of software agents and the proliferation of AI-generated content have weakened the reliability of digital actions as evidence of human involvement. Existing mechanisms, such as digital signatures and authentication protocols, verify identity and integrity, but do not establish whether a live human was present at the time an action was performed. In this paper, we introduce A-Tag, a system for verifiable human-in-the-loop tagging of digital artifacts. A-Tag cryptographically binds a file to a verified instance of live human presence at the moment of tagging. The resulting tag serves as a persistent and transferable proof that the action was triggered by a live human, without making claims about the origin, identity of the actor, or semantic content of the file. A-Tag is a modular framework combining liveness verification based on micro-motion signals shaped by human motor control, a secure cryptographic binding between the verified event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism enabling independent validation. We formalize security properties of human presence signals, define an adversarial model capturing automated and relay attacks, and analyze the system's guarantees and limitations. We implement A-Tag on commodity devices and evaluate it under realistic conditions. Our evaluation shows that A-Tag provides cryptographically sound artifact binding with deterministic verification, while enabling robust recovery under real-world transformations, achieving over 99 percent success for image-based artifacts, and maintaining sub-second verification and practical tagging latency.
entries.comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables

entries.title: Ties at the Top: A Point-in-Time Comparison of CVSS and EPSS at a Fixed Budget
entries.abstract: Organizations must decide which vulnerabilities warrant further analysis and protective action when the volume of published vulnerabilities exceeds their analytical capacity. We present a methodology for comparing vulnerability-prioritization strategies under an explicit resource constraint, represented by a fixed number of CVEs selected from a common eligible population. We apply this methodology to the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) and the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). For CVEs published in the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) from 17 March to 31 December 2025 and from 1 January to 31 March 2026 (Q1), we reconstruct each CVE's scores and status 30 days after NVD publication, using archived source data. Each cohort has one ranking per strategy at a 5% budget. Positives are CVEs added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within 180 days after their decision day. The catalog is maintained by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). EPSS captures 16 of 40 positives in 2025, versus 5 for CVSS; alternative selections among tied CVEs cannot raise CVSS capture above 9. In Q1, CVSS captures 4 of 11 and EPSS 3, but tie-breaking can reverse this ordering. The score alone leaves most of each CVSS list undecided: the tie-breaking rule allocates 1,678 of 1,919 CVSS places in 2025 and 589 of 758 in Q1 among CVEs tied at score 9.8. Most chosen CVSS scores come from non-NVD providers; disabling those scores reduces CVSS capture from 5 to 1 in 2025 and from 4 to 0 in Q1. A fixed-budget comparison should therefore report its decision cutoff, eligible population, score provenance, and tie-breaking rule.
entries.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures

entries.title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
entries.abstract: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

entries.title: Lossless Reversible Watermarking for AIGC with Applications in Authentication
entries.abstract: AIGC watermarking is commonly used for tracing, but it can also support applications such as authentication and tampering detection. We study lossless reversible watermarking, which enables exact recovery of the original watermarked image after permissible distortions. By exploiting the relatively low entropy of the information required for image generation, together with robust latent-space watermarking, we design a framework that preserves sufficient information for lossless recovery. We then apply the framework to AIGC authentication, which generally faces two key challenges. First, the authentication mechanism must resist adaptive adversaries. Second, the content relevant to authentication, such as visual designs or expressed messages, may depend on application requirements that are not known at generation time. To solve these difficulties, we incorporate cryptographic message authentication to provide unforgeability against adaptive attacks. Lossless recovery provides the original image as reference evidence, after which a suitable analyzer can be selected to make the authentication decision. Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery under a wide range of distortions.

entries.title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
entries.abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.
